explanations.explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees the “�” replacement‐character token (often in clusters), i.e. it flags spots where text contains unknown or mis-decoded characters (commonly at boundaries of foreign‐script or garbled input).
This neuron fires on base‐form “action” verbs (especially imperatives) that open instruction‐style sentences—words like “Convert,” “Put,” “Let,” etc.—marking command or directive contexts.
This feature flags emphatic or intensity-marking adverbs (e.g. “really,” “even,” “always,” “will,” “comes”)—words used to strengthen or spotlight a statement.

This neuron is looking for sentence- or clause-initial discourse pivots—adverbial “connective” words that signal contrast, concession or commentary (e.g. “However,” “Interestingly,” “Fortunately,” “Nevertheless,” etc.) often marked by a following comma.

This neuron isn’t tracking any real-world concept but rather the little “formatting” markers you see in scraped text (bold/italic delimiters, stray replacement‐character tokens that stand in for footnotes or citation anchors, etc.). It fires most strongly on the repeated “**�**�”-style tokens that bookend those annotations, signaling a shift in markup rather than any substantive content.

This neuron is basically an “H‐detector” – it spikes on the grapheme h (and h-containing clusters like “th”) across scripts (Latin h/H, Hangul ㅎ, Devanagari ह, etc.), i.e. the orthographic/phonetic marker for the /h/ sound.

This neuron fires on short subword units that sit at the ends of English words—especially two-letter, vowel-plus-consonant (or vowel-plus-consonant-consonant) “suffix-like” chunks (“ot,” “ul,” “or,” “ic,” “ew,” “end,” etc.).

This neuron is basically a “non-ASCII/foreign‐script” detector: it lights up on tokens that are accented Latin letters, ligatures or any non-Latin-alphabet characters (e.g. French Œ, Hungarian/Magyar accented vowels, Arabic, Hangul, Tamil, etc.), marking spans of text in other languages or with special Unicode glyphs.

This neuron fires on the main content word—the head noun or key lexical item—at the start of a title- or list-style phrase (i.e. the “topic” word immediately following an article in a heading or bullet).
This neuron is essentially a “list‐item/heading start” detector—it lights up on the very first word of a bullet or section‐header line, marking the boundary at the start of a new structured item.
This neuron fires on the period in the “U.S.” abbreviation—i.e. it marks references to the United States (typically in formal/governmental contexts).
This neuron flags stylized proper‐name tokens—i.e. sequences of capital (or otherwise non-standard) letters/characters used in brand names, acronyms, product titles or other named entities.
The feature is a dedicated detector for the subword “amenity” (often appearing as “Am en ity” in BPE form), i.e. it activates whenever the text refers to amenities or facility features.
This feature fires on the adversative discourse connector “However,” marking a contrastive turn or shift between clauses or sentences.

This neuron flags “non-standard” subword pieces – e.g. foreign-script characters or diacritic-rich/rare orthographic fragments (like Korean, Thai, Cyrillic, Devanagari, accented Latin, or uncommon English subwords such as “ith”).

This feature fires on capitalized sub-word pieces of named entities—especially proper surnames, place names and brand/organization names—marking tokens that form parts of people’s names, locations or company titles.
This feature fires on direct, second-person questions—especially headlines or ad-style prompts that begin with “Do you…” or “Could you…,” i.e. reader-addressing, call-to-action interrogatives.
This neuron fires whenever the model sees a short, all-caps (or mostly-caps) token or token sequence—i.e. acronyms, initialisms, product/model codes or other abbreviations used as names or labels.
This neuron flags occurrences of the abbreviation “U.S.”—i.e. it detects mentions of the United States via its period-separated short form.

This feature flags the very first, attention-grabbing word of a headline or bullet-point—typically an imperative or introductory keyword (Prepare, Choosing, Once, Routine, Treat, Replacement, etc.) that launches a new section or call-to-action.
